**Also closes #23997** — The local server sidecar health check failure cascades into MCP connection drops. When the app marks the sidecar as unhealthy, it tears down dependent MCP connections (Supabase, Desktop Commander, n8n, Universal Brain), while MCPs with their own persistent transport (Telegram, MetaTrader) survive. Fixing health check retry re-connects that circuit before the MCPs are torn down.

Steps to reproduce

2. Add a local project to the Desktop project list:
   /Users/oriondim/Documents/OpenCode_projects/simbrief-checklists
3. Open Edit Project for that project.

I experimented with this a bit. Just not at the level of 1 user - 1 pod/docker image. I think this setup is redundant and requires a lot of resources to maintain. I used one opencode server and multiple users, each with one session. Authentication is handled by the proxy layer. A session manager manages sessions. A separate folder is created for each user, where sessions and other files are stored. This can then be split into isolated S3 storage, for example. I also created my own UI client, since I wanted the simplest possible client without selecting a model or anything else, but that's not necessary. Overall, this setup works.

```
[Browser]
    |
    v
[Next.js web]
    |
    v
[FastAPI wrapper]
    |
    v
[Session manager]
    |
    v
[opencode serve per user]
    |
    v
[data/users/<user>/...]
```

This wasn't an OpenCode bug. OpenCode sends the model name as lower case. Our model look up was case sensitive. When we don't have the model requested, we default to MiniMax. We fixed this by making the model look up case insensitive. Why do we default to minimax? It fits comfortably on a minimum of 4 cards and the most stable model (its architecture so far just works out of the box with every optimization stably i.e. turboquant, LMCache, etc)

As we shuffle other models around during roll outs, it doesnt need to take up a whole b200 node on its own so we always have a replica of it live during these windows when something like an optimization for a different model crashes after roll out was marked successful. So when the lookup fails, it just defaults to minimax to keep requests flowing. 

Although we recently had to take down GPT OSS due to capacity constraints after the rush of new models during the last 2 weeks so if you're still calling that, it will default to minimax. We'll be bringing it back hopefully soon.

I manually tested all relevant Ollama endpoints with the same model and trivial prompt, and they all work correctly.

Successful manual tests:
- POST /v1/chat/completions -> 200 OK
- POST /v1/messages -> 200 OK
- POST /v1/messages?beta=true -> 200 OK

So this is not caused by:
- the endpoint path itself
- the `?beta=true` query parameter
- basic Ollama compatibility for these APIs

This strongly suggests Opencode is sending a problematic request payload or using a client-side flow that differs from the simple successful manual requests.

Given the Ollama logs also show:
- `aborting completion request due to client closing the connection`

the issue now looks much more like a Opencode request construction / streaming / tools / client-handling problem, not an Ollama endpoint problem.

These may be the same underlying bug or closely related manifestations worth investigating together.

I have also created [@gotgenes/opencode-session-context](https://github.com/gotgenes/opencode-session-context) for allowing other agents and subagents to access message history from arbitrary sessions, which, again, is useful for letting agents and subagents assess behavior and performance.

Thanks @luisifa for the pointer! I took a look at the plugin source.

The plugin wraps the provider fetch layer, caching and re-injecting actual thinking blocks (with signatures) across turns — that's a fundamentally different approach from our fix in `transform.ts` (which injects empty `reasoning_content: ""` unconditionally at the message serialization layer).

They're complementary:
- **Plugin**: preserves real thinking content for the model to reference, works at the HTTP layer
- **Our fix**: ensures API format compliance (every assistant message has `reasoning_content`), works at the message normalization layer

Going to test installing it today. If it works well, having both layers active means the plugin handles the rich thinking preservation and our fix acts as the fallback safeguard.

One question: does this plugin handle the case where history messages are replayed from DB (e.g. after Magic Context compression)? That's the specific path where we found `reasoning_content` gets dropped in DeepSeek's thinking mode — the fingerprint-based cache approach might miss on cold replay.

OSC 8 is the terminal escape sequence standard for clickable hyperlinks — it works even inside curses/alternate-screen applications because the terminal emulator handles the click, not the application.

The escape sequence format is:

```
\e]8;;https://example.com\e\\Link Text\e]8;;\e\\
```

Most modern terminals already support this (iTerm2, Kitty, WezTerm, Windows Terminal, GNOME VTE, foot, Warp, etc.). For terminals that don't, the escape is silently ignored and users just see the plain text — so it's backwards-compatible.

The Bubble Tea framework (which OpenCode uses) doesn't natively emit OSC 8, but you can inject the escape sequences when rendering any URL text in the TUI. The [charmbracelet/lipgloss](https://github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss) library has a `Hyperlink()` style method that does exactly this.

This would fix both this issue and #7273 (wrapped URLs breaking click detection), since OSC 8 links work regardless of line wrapping.
